title: "His Mother? Are You Mad?" Mouni Roy Heard the Whole Internet Laugh — and Decided She Didn't Care
excerpt: The Naagin star is exactly one year older than Varun Dhawan. She plays his fake mother in David Dhawan's latest. And her answer to the trolls is the most relaxed thing she's ever said.
body:
The joke writes itself, and the internet knew it before the film even opened. **Mouni Roy** — all smoky eyes and serpentine glamour, the woman who made a generation believe a shape-shifting snake could be the most desirable thing on Indian television — cast as the *mother* of **Varun Dhawan**, a man born a grand total of one calendar year after her. Twitter did the math in about four seconds. The memes arrived before the trailer finished buffering.

And here's the thing: she's in on it.

In **Hai Jawani Toh Ishq Hona Hai**, David Dhawan's deliriously old-school comedy of errors, Roy isn't anyone's real mother. She plays Rasmalai, an exotic dancer hired by Varun's character to *pose* as his mother — a fake matriarch conjured up to keep an elaborate web of lies intact for his new girlfriend's gangster brother. The gag, as one critic put it perfectly, is that the hero asked for a Nirupa Roy and the universe sent him a Mouni Roy instead. That's not a casting accident. That's the punchline.

> "People told me, 'Why are you playing Varun Dhawan's mother? Are you mad?'" — Mouni Roy, to News18

The trolling was, by all accounts, relentless. When the trailer dropped, social media couldn't get past the optics: a 40-year-old woman playing mother to a 39-year-old man, age difference of approximately one birthday. The makers got dragged. Roy got dragged harder. And somewhere in the middle of all that noise, she made a decision that's quietly become the most charming part of the whole circus.

"I can't do anything about it. I didn't care what the noise was," she told the channel. "It became such a big thing — 'how can the makers do this to me!' But I knew what I had done in the film. I knew that my director was very happy, and so is everybody I've worked with on the film." And then the line that's been making the rounds, delivered with the shrug of a woman who has nothing left to prove: **"If the role is good, I don't care."**

What makes this more than a standard-issue troll-clapback is how genuinely tickled Roy seems by the absurdity of it all. She admits her own first reaction matched everyone else's. When casting director **Mukesh Chhabra** first called, she heard "mother" and balked. "My first reaction was also that. I was like, 'His mother?'" she recalled. It took a narration from David Dhawan himself, plus dialogue writer **Farhad Samji**, to flip her perspective — and once she got the joke, she got it completely. "I found it hilarious! Just picture Varun calling Maniesh and saying, 'I don't want just a mother's phone call; I need a full-fledged mother, like Nirupa Roy.' Then there's a scene where someone questions whether I'm too short to play a mother."

This is, remarkably, Roy's first proper comedy. The woman built her career on slithering menace — *Naagin*, the icy sorceress Junoon in *Brahmastra* — and on the kind of dance numbers that stop a room. Slapstick was never her register. She's described David Dhawan's filmography as her "comfort watch," the comedies she returns to when the world is too much, and there's something almost sweet about a femme-fatale specialist finally getting to be silly. She also made a shrewd promotional call: she stayed almost entirely out of the marketing campaign, keeping Rasmalai a surprise. "It made people curious about what I'm doing in the film," she noted — and curiosity, in a summer this crowded, is currency.

The film itself, released June 5, has been a polarizing beast — a David Dhawan entertainer in the fullest, most chaotic sense, all boomer humour and forced wokeness wrestling each other to a draw, with Varun fronting a plot involving simultaneous pregnancies, a London fling, and the aforementioned fake-mother gambit. Critics weren't kind. Audiences, however, kept showing up: the film posted strong weekday holds and is eyeing a lifetime north of ₹60 crore, a respectable number for a mid-budget comedy in a year of ₹300-crore epics. **Mrunal Thakur** and **Pooja Hegde** play the two women, with a roll-call of comic veterans — Johny Lever, Rajpal Yadav, Chunky Panday — filling out the noise.

For the diaspora, *Hai Jawani Toh Ishq Hona Hai* is the kind of film that plays best on a Friday night with low expectations and a high tolerance for chaos. It's available in theatres across the US, UK and Canada, with a digital premiere expected to follow in the coming weeks — watch JioHotstar, where most Taurani-produced titles eventually land.

As for Roy: she walked into the internet's loudest punchline, looked it dead in the eye, and laughed first. At 40, playing a 39-year-old's mother, refusing to apologize for either number — honestly, that's the most magnetic she's been in years.
